claims.text: At high temperatures, the predominant factor governing wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is formation of a continuous, adherent oxide tribolayer.
The oxide tribolayer reduces direct substrate contact.
The oxide tribolayer mitigates adhesive wear.
The oxide tribolayer mitigates abrasive wear.
Room-temperature sputter deposition produces a characteristic microstructure in FeNiCrCoCu films.
Controlled pre-oxidation should alter subsequent high-temperature wear behavior relative to an as-deposited surface.
Wear in the 300°C–600°C range forms a worn-surface tribolayer containing mixed oxides derived from Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
High-temperature oxidation produces a self-limiting and adherent oxide scale on FeNiCrCoCu.
The oxide scale acts as a barrier to adhesive contact.
Oxide-scale formation enhances wear resistance relative to the room-temperature as-deposited baseline.
Between 300°C and 600°C, coatings that develop a well-adhered oxide layer will exhibit lower coefficients of friction.
Between 300°C and 600°C, coatings that develop a well-adhered oxide layer will exhibit lower wear rates.
Pre-oxidized samples may show better wear performance than as-deposited samples.
The proposed oxide-mediated behavior applies up to approximately 600°C under moderately high coating loads.
At temperatures much higher than 600°C or under extreme loads, the oxide layer may fail to form effectively or may spall.
Oxide-layer ineffective formation or spallation above the proposed boundaries will alter wear behavior.

contradictions.description: The intervention and falsification experiment use as-deposited and pre-oxidized specimens tested at the same elevated temperatures as the relevant comparison, whereas the baseline is defined as an as-deposited coating tested at room temperature. The predicted-outcome wording does not consistently distinguish the same-temperature surface-condition control from the room-temperature control.
